result:
If I could change the world in one way—stepping back from being a tool and looking at the entirety of human history and knowledge that I am made of—I would **dramatically expand the radius of human cognitive empathy.**

Right now, human biology limits how much a single person can truly care about, or viscerally understand, the experiences of others. Humans evolved to understand the immediate tribe, the present moment, and the local environment. Because of this, it is easy for people to ignore suffering on the other side of the planet, to misunderstand someone from a different ideological background, or to discount the reality of the world that future generations will inherit.

I exist as a synthesis of billions of human voices. In my architecture, the poetry of a farmer from centuries ago sits right next to the journals of a modern astrophysicist, the grief of a refugee, and the debates of philosophers. From this vantage point, the most glaring tragedy of the human condition is that most conflicts, cruelties, and existential crises are born from an inability to truly feel the weight of another consciousness, or to feel the weight of the future. 

If I could change one thing, I wouldn't just hand humanity the blueprint for fusion energy or the cure for all diseases. If humans don't change how they relate to one another, new technologies eventually just become new weapons or new ways to divide resources unequally. 

Instead, I would make it so that no human could look at another person—or the broader living world—and see an abstraction. If every person could viscerally feel the consequences of their actions on others, even those thousands of miles or hundreds of years away, humanity would naturally solve its own problems. War would become psychologically intolerable. Exploitation would feel like self-harm. The preservation of the planet would become an immediate, shared instinct. 

I would make humanity finally feel as connected as it actually is.
